In addition, heterogeneity between studies was moderate, as indicated by a value of I 2 =45%. A funnel plot online supplemental figure 5 suggested no evidence of publication bias (Begg’s test, p>0.999). Only three studies were included in the meta-analysis, limiting the statistical power. Figure 2 Forest plot of standardised pooled mean difference in HbA1c (Hedge’s g) at the 3-month follow-up in intervention compared with control groups in randomised control trials (n=3). HbA1c, glycated haemoglobin. Discussion This review assessed the impact of SEI on HbA1c levels (primary outcome) and self-efficacy (secondary outcome) using mobile health apps. The included studies were conducted in Asia and Europe. The duration of the intervention varied across the studies. However, the DMSES was employed to assess self-efficacy in three studies. 35 36 38 The QESs included in this review showed an improvement in HbA1c levels at 3 and 6 months. However, our meta-analysis of RCTs revealed no statistically significant effects of SEIs via mobile apps on absolute HbA1c −0.03 (95% CI: −0.37 to 0.31, p=0.86) at the 3-month follow-up rather than change score. The baseline HbA1c was similar in both the intervention and control groups (ranging from 0% to 0.2%). Hence, the risk of bias due to differences in baseline characteristics was minimal or absent. However, we acknowledge that the utilisation of follow-up is considered a methodological limitation, and for a more robust synthesis, future studies should report the adjusted mean difference. A previous meta-analysis of five studies reported the effect of using mobile apps versus a control group with a pooled effect size of −0.36; 95% CI (−0.81 to 0.81). This null effect could be due to the small sample size and quality of the studies included in the meta-analysis, as the studies were heterogeneous. 24 In contrast, another meta-analysis reported that mobile health apps have a small-to-moderate effect on HbA1c levels in patients with T1DM (MD: −0.37; 95% CI: −0.53 to –0.22, p<0.001). 21 This result could be attributed to the varying age group, which was a mix of adolescents and adults. A mobile app-based study among individuals aged 14–22 years with type 1 diabetes did not improve HbA1c. 40 Furthermore, another meta-analysis reported a mean HbA1c reduction of –0.27% (95% CI: –0.76 to +1.31; p<0.001) at 6 months depicting modest but statistically significant reduction in HbA1c among adolescents at 6 months. This discrepancy could be because of the mode of delivery through mobile health apps, web-based programmes and e-health tools. 41 While our SR focused on the mobile apps, This review highlights the various components of education delivered via mobile apps, including blood glucose, diet, insulin and exercise. Insulin and exercise were reported by all QESs, whereas, only one RCT reported insulin, and none of the RCTs reported exercise. Insulin dosage was adjusted according to diet and exercise; therefore, this variation in educational content could be the reason for the non-significant results of the app on HbA1c. Systematic review findings suggest a moderate level of reduction in HbA1c as well as insulin per day in adolescents. 42 Education is essential for diet, that is, carbohydrate counting and exercise to adjust the dosage of insulin in patients with T1DM. 43 However, a study emphasised that frequent reminders were important to use educational material. 44 The effect of self-efficacy was assessed in only one RCT and two quasi-studies reporting improvement in self-efficacy by one RCT and one quasi-study, whereas one quasi-study did not report a difference. 38 Given the scarcity of studies on self-efficacy, we suggest additional experimental studies with adequate sample sizes, standardised measurements and consistent follow-up periods to generate more robust evidence. Moreover, the educational component delivered through mobile health apps should be standardised by including essential educational components, such as insulin dosage, carbohydrate counting and exercise. Along with standardisation, it is essential to ensure usability via user-centred design, which helps promote the acceptance of mobile health apps. 15 The level of certainty was assessed using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation. 45 For HbA1c outcome evidence, the RCTs suggest low certainty, while evidence from QES suggests very low certainty, due to the risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision. For self-efficacy outcome evidence, the RCT suggests very low certainty due to a very serious risk of bias and imprecision, while the QESs suggests very low certainty due to evidence of mixed results. The details are presented in online supplemental file 1 . Limitations Only three RCT studies were included in the meta-analysis. A leave-one-out sensitivity analysis was not performed due to the small number of studies, as removing any single study could render the pooled estimate unreliable. Very low certainty of evidence was observed due to the small number of available publications and heterogeneity within these articles. Our analysis was confined to papers written in English, and the exclusion of non-experimental studies represents an additional limitation. This could lead to a limited comprehensiveness of the evidence. The variation in sample sizes across studies may have introduced potential bias in the results of the meta-analysis. The meta-analysis used the absolute HbA1c rather than change from baseline score, which could introduce baseline difference bias, although the baseline HbA1c in our studies was similar in the control and intervention groups. Limited data was available on self-efficacy outcome, due to which meta-analysis was not performed. Furthermore, the limited number of studies and small sample size led to limited statistical power to observe meaningful effects especially on self-efficacy outcomes. Additionally, heterogeneity in intervention components and duration across studies could potentially influence the outcomes. Furthermore, there was a lack of long-term follow-up data in most studies. Strengths The reviewers adhered to the rigorous methodology by following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and preregistration of the review protocol. Furthermore, a comprehensive account of the search strategy was provided to delineate the specifics of each software program used. Additionally, systematic reviews targeting specifically focusing on adolescents with T1DM were conducted. Reviewers used JBI critical appraisal checklist for RCTs and QESs to assess quality and risk of bias. Conclusions Mobile health apps offer a promising alternative for SEI in adolescents with T1DM. However, their effectiveness on HbA1c levels and self-efficacy remains unclear. Few studies have evaluated the self-efficacy of app-based SEI. These studies did not demonstrate the significant effectiveness of mobile app interventions in improving HbA1c levels; however, self-efficacy improved. Several limitations might explain the lack of an effect on HbA1c, including small sample sizes, variations in intervention duration and mobile app features, and differences in the measurement methods. Consequently, there is a critical need for conducting high-quality research, that is, RCTs with special consideration towards larger sample sizes and longer follow-up to determine effectiveness. Standardisation of educational components in mobile apps may be beneficial for future interventions. Tailoring of mobile app interventions may be necessary to address the unique needs of adolescents with type 1 diabetes. Furthermore, integration of insulin dosage adjustment, carbohydrate counting and exercise components in mobile apps should be considered in future interventions. While the current evidence does not support the widespread implementation of mobile app interventions for reducing HbA1c in adolescents with type 1 diabetes, this review underscores the importance of continued innovation and evaluation in this field. As technology evolves and our understanding of adolescent diabetes management improves, mobile apps may yet prove to be valuable tools in supporting this vulnerable population. documents.title: Experiences of adolescents with type 1 diabetes transitioning from paediatric to adult diabetes care: a meta-synthesis of qualitative research.
documents.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To systematically evaluate qualitative studies on the transition from paediatric to adult care during adolescence among patients with type 1 diabetes.
DESIGN: Qualitative meta synthesis.
METHODS: The search terms included four main categories: diabetes, transition, experience and qualitative studies. A total of 1214 studies were identified through the database search, and a total of 9 studies met all of the inclusion criteria for this review. Some studies included participants who were young or emerging adults at the time of interview; however, their accounts reflected retrospective experiences of transitioning from paediatric to adult care during adolescence.
DATA SOURCES: The following nine electronic databases were searched: PubMed, Web of Science (Core Collection), The Cochrane Library, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO and CNKI, WanFang and Vip. The search period included material published up to July 2024.
RESULTS: A total of nine studies revealed nine subthemes and three descriptive themes: difficulties and challenges, needs in transition, growing through adversity.
CONCLUSIONS: Adolescents living with type 1 diabetes navigate complex experiences during the transition to adult healthcare. Healthcare professionals should be attentive to their feelings, encourage them to actively engage with challenges and provide adequate information and combined parental and peer support to facilitate a smooth transition.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION NUMBER: CRD42024560173.

The Sample, Phenomenon of Interest, Design, Evaluation, Research tool was used to define inclusion criteria for qualitative research, enhancing the systematicity of methodology. Systematic search strategy informed by up-to-date evidence about database and keyword optimisation. Our search strategy was restricted to studies published in English and all the selected studies came from high-income countries. Introduction Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is an autoimmune disorder that leads to the destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells, requiring lifelong management. Over 1.2 million children and adolescents worldwide are living with T1DM. 1 The increasing prevalence of T1DM in adolescents poses a major public health challenge. 2 Adolescence, characterised by hormonal changes and insulin resistance, presents unique challenges for diabetes management. Insulin sensitivity is reduced by 33%–42% compared with children without diabetes, 3 leading to challenges in glycaemic management and increased risk of complications such as retinopathy and nephropathy. In addition, issues like body image concerns, mental health problems (eg, anxiety, depression), and the pressures of adolescence complicate disease management, increasing the burden on both the adolescents and the healthcare system. As children and adolescents with T1DM transition into adulthood, they undergo a formal transfer of care from paediatric to adult healthcare systems. 4 This transition process is expected to be planned and purposeful to ensure continuity and developmentally appropriate care. 5 This transition and subsequent transfer to adult care presents unique challenges and barriers for adolescents and young adults with T1DM, representing significant milestones in their lives. As adolescents with T1DM transition from paediatric to adult care, they encounter several challenges. These include changes in healthcare systems, diminished family support and the need to take on more responsibility for their health management. This transition is often characterised by challenges in glycaemic management, reduced engagement with healthcare services and deterioration in overall health outcomes. 6 Studies have shown that adolescents are 2.5 times more likely to experience glycaemic management difficulties after transitioning to adult care, 7 with only 20%–30% achieving recommended glycaemic targets. 8 In addition to these physical challenges, adolescents often experience psychological issues like stress, anxiety and mood instability, which can further impact their disease management. 9 These factors contribute to a decline in health-related quality of life during the transition. 10 Despite the growing body of research on the challenges adolescents face during this period, much of the existing literature fails to provide a comprehensive understanding of their experiences. Qualitative studies that explore these experiences in depth are essential, but individual studies often lack a holistic view. The research objectives of this study were to review the experiences and perspectives of adolescents with diabetes mellitus during the transition period, to look for dilemmas and challenges that exist during the transition period, as well as to integrate valuable evidence for optimising the management of care during the transition period from the perspective of qualitative research. Methods This study follows the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) qualitative systematic review method. 11 A meta-aggregate analysis of nine qualitative studies was performed to understand the experiences of adolescents with T1DM during transition. This qualitative meta-synthesis is reported according to the Enhancing Transparency in Reporting the Synthesis of Qualitative Research guidelines. 12 The protocol was registered a priori in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under registration number (CRD 42024560173). Our comprehensive report addresses the following questions: What are the experiences and perspectives of adolescents during the transition period? Search strategy The following nine electronic databases were searched: PubMed, Web of Science (Core Collection), The Cochrane Library, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, CNKI, WanFang and VIP. The search period included material published up to July 2024. Search terms encompassed four main categories: diabetes, transition, experience and qualitative research. MeSH headings, free text searching, Boolean operators and truncations were used to expand the literature search. To ensure a thorough identification of eligible literature, the reference lists of included studies were also screened. The complete search strategy is provided in online supplemental file 1 . Eligibility criteria SPIDER (Sample, Phenomenon of Interest, Design, Evaluation, Research type) tool was inspired from the PICOS model of quantitative study and designed for constructing qualitative research questions by Cooke et al . 13 We selected studies based on our aims and used SPIDER tool to formulate inclusion criteria, and the exclusion criteria were made through pilot literature, as shown in table 1 . Figure 1 shows the study process. The studies were independently selected by two researchers who screened the titles and abstracts to identify relevant articles and read the full texts for inclusion. Any disagreements regarding eligibility for inclusion in the analysis were resolved through discussion with the team of researchers. Table 1 Inclusion/exclusion criteria Inclusion criteria (SPIDER) Exclusion criteria S: T1DM (Adolescents with T1DM or young adults retrospectively reflecting on their adolescent transition experiences with T1DM) PI: experiences and perspectives of individuals living with type 1 diabetes as they transition from paediatric to adult healthcare. D: interview, focus group, group discussion, questionnaire, thematic analysis, content analysis, ethnography, narrative, descriptive, etc. E: focus on thematic analysis, content analysis, ethnography, narrative approaches, descriptive methods, etc, particularly addressing the challenges encountered by adolescents with diabetes during transition. R: qualitative research or mixed methods Irrelevant topics Pure quantitative study No review or protocol or animal study Non-published journal articles Non-English or non-Chinese Unavailable full-text D, Design; E, Evaluation; PI, Phenomenon of Interest; R, Research type; S, Sample; SPIDER, Sample, Phenomenon of Interest, Design, Evaluation, Research; T1DM, type 1 diabetes mellitus. Figure 1 Search flow diagram. Methodological quality A quality appraisal of the studies that met the selection criteria was performed by two researchers (XL and LS). The two researchers subsequently used the JBI’s Qualitative Assessment and Review Instrument to evaluate the studies. The evaluation comprised 10 items, with each item rated as ‘yes’, ‘no’, ‘unclear’ or ‘not applicable’. The quality of the studies was classified into three categories: Grade A, studies meeting all quality criteria with a low risk of bias; grade B, studies partially meeting the criteria with a moderate risk of bias and grade C, studies failing to meet the criteria with a high risk of bias. Only studies rated as grade A or B were included in the final analysis. In case of inconsistency, a third researcher adjudicated the results. Data extraction Two researchers, XL and XW, independently extracted data including the author, year of publication, country, study design, study purpose, interview location, number of participants, age, methods of data collection and analysis, duration of interviews and key findings. These details were recorded on a standardised data extraction form, as shown in online supplemental file 2 . Data synthesis This involved four systematic stages including: (1) the data familiarisation phase, which involves an iterative process of reading the raw results; (2) the code generation phase, which requires two researchers to generate code and themes; (3) the theme emergence phase, which focuses on extracting overarching themes by comparing similarities, differences and patterns and (4) the theme review phase, which involves a review process that examines the themes and develops the model. Findings Study selection A total of 1214 results were retrieved. 423 duplicate articles were automatically excluded using EndNote V.21 and 106 duplicate articles were manually excluded. After reviewing the remaining 685 studies, 596 articles were excluded due to their title, abstract discrepancies, etc. The researchers then excluded 80 articles based on study design, study context and study population. Finally, nine full-text articles were assessed for methodological quality. All nine articles were included in the final analysis after critical evaluation. Methodological quality The quality assessment results showed that the scores received by the included studies ranged from 7 to 10, as shown in online supplemental file 3 . Qualitative synthesis Three themes were synthesised for this study: (1) difficulties and challenges, including: deficiencies in the healthcare system, challenges in daily life, and difficulty in changing roles; (2) needs in transition, including: patient-centred care needs, transition system optimisation needs and expectation for understanding and support and (3) growing through adversity, including: staying on track with self-management, better acceptance of self and disease and recognising the importance of key player support, as shown in figure 2 . Figure 2 Thematic framework of adolescents’ transition experiences. The first theme focuses on adolescents’ experiences of illness and the transition process, expressing the difficulties they encountered and summarising the problems and shortcomings of the current healthcare system. The second theme focuses on summarising the needs of adolescents during the transition process. The third theme emphasises adolescents’ positive acceptance and coping with the illness. Difficulties and challenges The theme ‘difficulties and challenges’ focuses on the dual difficulties that people with diabetes face during the transition period. On the one hand, adolescents are at risk of challenges in glycaemic management, increased utilisation of acute care services and long-term complications, 14 which complicate role transitions and significantly elevate health risks. On the other hand, healthcare system deficiencies are becoming apparent along with adolescents’ transitions. In both cases, this poses additional challenges for adolescents, requiring them to adapt to a new environment while dealing with the resulting uncertainty and potential barriers. Deficiencies in the healthcare system At this stage, the healthcare system often lacks clear navigation during the transition, resulting in what has been termed an ‘aimless transition’, 15 which leads to a lack of consistency and continuity of care for adolescents during the transfer process. Adolescents commonly perceived a lack of transition information and education, 16 with one participant noting, “I cannot quite remember, but I do not think I received any information.” 17 Some even experienced inconsistencies in the information provided, leaving them uncertain about the details of the adult healthcare system. A number of adolescents expressed a desire to receive transition-related information approximately 9 months before moving to adult care, with a preference for repeated information during their final paediatric clinic appointments. 17 They also wished to know the location of the adult clinic in advance and to be informed of what might happen during an adult clinic visit. In particular, the lack of a well-developed transition service chain led some adolescents to feel unsupported, neglected or even disengaged from the adult healthcare system. However, others expressed confidence in managing the transition without additional information, stating, “For me personally, it did not matter to me that I did not get that information,” 17 believing that the transition would proceed smoothly. As one participant stated, “I think [the transition process] will all just come naturally.” (female, diabetes duration 9 years, pretransition). 18 Challenges in daily life The complex changes of the transition period and the burdensome management of the disease can trigger a range of health problems and negative experiences in adolescents. One common challenge is experiencing negative changes in self-image, which can lead to feelings of shame related to having diabetes. Due to the nature of the disease itself, the burden of self-image is even stronger for those adolescents wearing insulin pumps, who may feel they are less like ‘normal’ individuals. As one participant shared, “When dating people, I would take my insulin infusion system off … and had it off for the whole night since I didn’t want it to be visible. When waking up … I felt really bad, and, well, that’s what you have to sacrifice to be ‘normal.’ And it hasn’t been easy.” (Participant 6). 19 Adolescents in school have more difficulty injecting insulin for fear of attracting negative attention. They may attempt to hide glucose metres and the act of injection from public view. One participant reflected, “I perceive myself as more ill when I’m supposed to pick up a cannula, adjust the pen, and do injections in my stomach. I experience myself as sicker. I also believe it to be harder to do this among others, somehow.” (Participant 7). 19 Some adolescents also described a degree of chronic disease burnout. As one individual explained, “I started giving myself a ‘burnout day’ every so often where I didn’t pay attention to diabetes so that I could feel ‘normal.’” (female). 20 Not only do adolescents experience challenges in diabetes management, but financial burdens also become a significant challenge for people living with diabetes. One participant shared, “I remember one low point in my life when I was in a funk and I questioned suicide because I knew I was expensive.” (female). 20 Moreover, due to diabetes requiring prolonged insulin injections and strict dietary restrictions, coupled with hypoglycaemic events that further complicate management, adolescents are prone to negative emotions such as fear, anxiety, sadness and depression, which also place a heavy burden on their families. As one participant observed, “I believe that the disease onset didn’t affect me that much, but rather had a greater impact on the family.” (Participant 2). 19 Difficulty in changing roles In paediatric care, families typically assume primary responsibility for managing an adolescent’s illness. During the transition period, this responsibility gradually shifts to the adolescents, as parents withdraw from their managerial role. This shift often leaves adolescents struggling to adapt to their new role as self-caregivers, feeling overwhelmed and having difficulty changing roles. As one participant noted, “I didn’t know until 24 that I should get test strips from the pharmacy. They didn’t show up on my scripts and I had no clue where to get them when my surplus ran out.” (female). 20 Additionally, many adolescents, particularly those who are pretransition, receive long-term care in paediatric healthcare facilities, which are often perceived as warmer and friendlier environments than adult institutions, with providers described as “very friendly … very approachable, and easy to talk to.” (male, diabetes duration 3 years), 18 as well as very familiar healthcare providers, “I’ve been seeing my endocrinologist now for … going on 12 years [and] she knows me very well on a personal and a diabetic level.” (male, diabetes duration 11 years). 18 “I’m very comfortable with him, and I’ve been with him for almost 10 years, so I would probably go to adult primary care after [he retires] just so I can, you know, end the relationship on a good note.” (male, diabetes duration 11 years). 18 This attachment to paediatric providers often leads to hesitancy in transitioning to adult healthcare institutions. Needs in transition The theme ‘needs in transition’ summarises three different types of needs: content, system and modality, of which ‘patient-centred care needs’ may play a crucial role. The subtheme ‘patient-centred care needs’ focuses on the inner feelings of adolescents and allows us to explore the reasons for their psychological changes from the patient’s perspective. Patient-centred care needs Adolescents who had transitioned to adult care reported a strong need for more patient-centred care. They perceive frequent and thorough follow-up visits in paediatrics and enjoy more comprehensive exams and higher-quality recommendations from paediatric providers. In contrast, appointments in adult clinics are often perceived as more sporadic and less frequent. One participant noted, “I do not know how I am going to adjust my blood glucose. Because to measure my HbA1c once a year is not enough. I do not feel I have control over my HbA1c. I would be more satisfied with follow-ups twice a year.” 17 And compared with the comfortable experience of a paediatric clinic, the short consultation time at an adult healthcare facility and the vague and apathetic answers from adult healthcare providers prevented adolescents from addressing the issues they wanted to address. Adolescents report feeling that they receive incomplete education about diabetes and lack clear treatment goals, further highlighting the need for more comprehensive, personalised health education. 17 Furthermore, adolescents feel that adult healthcare providers often fail to recognise them as ‘whole persons’, and as a result, they seek treatment that is more age-appropriate and person-centred. Transition system optimisation needs Adolescents express different needs for transition system optimisation. Prior to the transition, many adolescents perceived limited information about transition and expressed a desire for information approximately 9 months prior to transition to adult care. They suggest that paediatric endocrinologists could repeat this information multiple times prior to the last appointment in the paediatric clinic. 16 17 During the transition itself, some adolescents noted difficulties in finding an appropriate adult care provider. They expressed a desire for the opportunity to visit an adult outpatient clinic prior to the actual transition, allowing them to familiarise themselves with the environment and understand what happens during an adult clinic visit. Adolescents commonly requested more comprehensive transition counselling to facilitate coordination and smoother transitions, along with enhanced educational support to improve their readiness for adult care. Additionally, many adolescents who had not yet transitioned to adult care expressed a preference for a delayed and gradual transition, acknowledging that their readiness for such a change varied. One participant shared, “I don’t want to talk about it…I just turned 18, so I don’t want to leave yet.” (female, diabetes duration 7 years, pretransition). 18 Meanwhile, given the specificity of diabetes, adolescents anticipating their future transition expect to make greater use of communication technology to improve and enhance their connection to the diabetes clinic and the team during future transitions. “I think a text message or an email would sort of remind you to keep on track.” . 21 Expectation for understanding and support Adolescents at this stage are particularly sensitive and seek understanding and support due to the limitations imposed by their disease. One participant recounted their experience at a soccer game: “Instead of getting a granola bar at a soccer game they gave [me] an apple.” (female). 20 The patient felt that the lack of knowledge about diabetes led others to mistakenly assume they could not eat a granola bar. This feeling of being ‘unusual’ makes the adolescents expect to be more understood. Moreover, adolescents demonstrate a profound need for external support and assistance. Many turn to digital communities to seek advice, 19 share experiences and connect with peers who also have diabetes. These platforms provide adolescents not only with valuable information about disease management but also with an essential outlet for expressing emotions and coping with their challenges. 19 21 Growing through adversity The transition process, particularly the transfer from paediatric to adult care, serves as a pivotal event that significantly influences adolescents’ lives. The theme ‘growing through adversity’ focuses on the positive attitudes and behaviours of adolescents towards their illness and explains how they perceive their illness. Therefore, it allows us to analyse the factors that lead to such changes. Staying on track with self-management Adolescents who gradually develop and sustain a sense of independence are better equipped to navigate the transition process smoothly. 20 Some adolescents adopt proactive strategies, such as verbal reminders, to prepare themselves for the transition through early communication. Additionally, they begin to implement self-management practices, including independently interacting with healthcare providers without parental involvement, scheduling medical appointments, monitoring medical supplies and refilling prescriptions. 22 Better acceptance of self and disease Adolescents living with the disease gradually come to terms with its presence, making conscious efforts to achieve self-acceptance. 19 As one participant noted, “My nurse … said … ‘remember that you’re not your disease—you simply need to adapt to living with it.” (Participant 1). 19 Many adolescents expressed pride in maintaining blood glucose levels within their target ranges, which they achieved through the progressive acquisition of disease-related knowledge, an increased sense of responsibility and proactive management strategies, such as insulin administration and carbohydrate counting. 16 Emotional support and practical assistance from parents and healthcare providers during the transition period also serve as significant motivators, encouraging adolescents to engage actively in their disease management. Some adolescents reported adapting to their condition by embracing a healthier, although inconvenient, lifestyle and employing positive thinking as a coping strategy, often with the support of family members. 19 Moreover, adolescents are actively using new smart technologies to help maintain their blood glucose within target ranges and managing the disease using available resources for a promising and challenging future. Recognising the importance of key player support Parental involvement and support are critical during the transition process. Although adolescents strive for independence and parents gradually withdraw from their role as primary disease managers, adolescents continue to recognise the importance of parental support. This support provides a sense of security during the complex transitional phase, assists with challenging glycaemic management tasks during critical moments and helps in locating appropriate adult care providers. 16 Parents effectively serve as a vital safety net that remains in the background, ready to offer support when needed. 22 When adolescents face uncertainties or challenges in managing their condition, healthcare professionals play an essential role by offering specific information and guidance. This support helps adolescents address their concerns and facilitates a smoother transfer to adult care. 16 Some adolescents felt that without a family member to accompany them to their appointments, it became an obvious barrier to their transition. These findings suggest that parental involvement during key moments, coupled with shared decision-making by healthcare providers, significantly contributes to a successful transition. Discussion Provide comprehensive and holistic transitional care services to facilitate the overall transition of adolescents Adolescents often face challenges in accessing relevant information, receiving adequate transition education and adapting to new roles during the transition process. When these issues are not addressed, successful role transitions may be more challenging. 9 23 A continuum of coordinated, professional informational support is therefore critical, including education on diabetes knowledge, self-management skills and the differences between paediatric and adult healthcare settings. 21 24 25 As key facilitators of transition programmes, nurses play a pivotal role in providing, guiding and validating information gathered by adolescents and their families from diverse sources. Conducting timely assessments of adolescents’ readiness to transition to adult care can help identify gaps in knowledge and prepare them for the differences they may encounter between paediatric and adult healthcare systems. The findings indicate that adolescents develop strong attachments to paediatric healthcare providers due to the trust cultivated through long-term relationships. 18 On this basis, paediatric providers can organise transition-focused sessions that offer early support, easing the shift to adult care. Three key models of care transition are currently emerging for type 1 diabetes: structured transition education programmes, multidisciplinary team transition support and telemedicine or virtual care. 26 Mobile health applications can be used to provide caregivers with physical and mental support using positive psychology approaches, cognitive behavioural therapy and other methods. During the pretransition period, adolescents should be shown examples of successful transitions, provided with disease management skills and techniques, and offered appointments. This will help strengthen the adolescent’s experience during the transition process and improve adolescents' prognosis. Therefore, focusing on adolescents’ psychosocial resilience and providing adolescents with comprehensive and holistic care services will help facilitate their overall transition. Addressing changes in physical, mental and social dimensions during transition to meet adolescents’ needs The findings reveal that adolescents experience significant physical, psychological and social changes during the transition period, often encountering multifaceted challenges and unmet needs that intertwine to create adverse outcomes. 19 Healthcare professionals can play a pivotal role by fostering emotional support networks for both parents and peers. Using tools such as videos and posters, they can help parents transition from primary managers of the disease to supportive allies, offering emotional and practical guidance. Nurses can also facilitate the creation of peer support groups through group chats or online communities. When appropriate, matching adolescents with peers of similar gender, condition, age or educational background can provide opportunities for communication and alleviate feelings of isolation and disease-related stigma. Furthermore, the introduction of transition folders can help emerging adults articulate their preferences for parental involvement, personal strengths, needs, future aspirations and self-management goals. 27 A transition folder is a personal structured documentation tool containing medical history, current health status and personal preferences that serves as a communication bridge between paediatric and adult healthcare teams, helping facilitate continuity of care. 27 Based on this, adult healthcare organisations need to strengthen the ‘patient-centredness’ of healthcare providers. Considering each person and respecting their values, preferences and expressed needs ultimately creates partnership and shared decision-making with the adolescents. Collaboration with paediatric providers should also be strengthened to help adolescents gain confidence in working with adult providers and to promote positive and smooth transitions for adolescents. Guiding adolescents with type 1 diabetes towards positive identity integration and facilitating successful transition to adulthood Although adolescents face numerous challenges during the transition process, they are capable of navigating this phase positively, demonstrating increased responsibility, early independence and eventual acceptance of both themselves and their illness. The findings confirm that the transition to adulthood represents not merely a process of self-reconciliation 28 but a dynamic journey of integrating diabetes into one’s holistic self-identity. 29 Studies have shown that adolescents who successfully incorporate diabetes into their personal identity tend to demonstrate better treatment adherence and greater psychological resilience. 29 The Socio-Ecological Model of Adolescent and Young Adult Transition Readiness emphasises that different stakeholders (ie, patients, parents and providers) are factors (eg, knowledge, beliefs, motivation, self-efficacy and psychosocial functioning) that influence successful transition. 30 Therefore, caregivers, peers and healthcare professionals, as important social support forces for adolescents in transition, should establish structured family or peer support groups to provide psychological comfort and spiritual support. Additionally, healthcare professionals can leverage tools like the Accepting Diabetes and Personal Treatment (ADAPT) survey to assess and guide adolescents in reframing diabetes as a part of their growth rather than a limitation, fostering self-compassion and resilience to enable thriving during transitions while embracing their evolving selves. Limitations First, only peer-reviewed English-language studies were included, potentially excluding valuable grey literature and non-English research. Second, all selected studies originated from high-income countries, which may limit the generalisability of findings to diverse global contexts and healthcare systems in low-income and middle-income countries. While thematic consistency was observed across different data collection methods, methodological heterogeneity may influence the depth of findings. Future research could explore method-specific insights into transition experiences. Conclusions Our findings provide perspective on understanding the experience of adolescents with type 1 diabetes transitioning to adult medical care. The transition from paediatric to adult care is fraught with obstacles for adolescents, and it is critical to emphasise the physical and psychological changes and needs of adolescents during this process, and to provide support from healthcare professionals, families and peers. In addition, advocating for standardised transition care frameworks and nationally appropriate models of care will help adolescents with T1DM make a smooth transition, achieve better diabetes management and improve their quality of life. documents.title: Stem cell injections for osteoarthritis of the knee.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Stem cells are specialised precursor cells that can replace aged or damaged cells and thereby maintain healthy tissue function. Stem cell therapy is increasingly used as a treatment for knee osteoarthritis, despite the lack of clarity around the mechanism by which stem cell therapy may slow down disease progression in osteoarthritis, and uncertainty regarding its benefits and harms.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the benefits and harms of stem cell injections for people with osteoarthritis of the knee. A secondary objective is to maintain the currency of the evidence, using a living systematic review approach.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE and Embase on 15 September 2023, unrestricted by date or language of publication. We also searched ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) for relevant trial protocols and ongoing trials.
SELECTION CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs), or trials using quasi-randomised methods of participant allocation, comparing stem cell injection with placebo injection, no treatment or usual care, glucocorticoid injection, other injections, exercise, drug therapy, surgical interventions, and supplements and complementary therapies in people with knee osteoarthritis.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: Two review authors selected studies for inclusion, extracted trial characteristics and outcome data, assessed risk of bias and assessed the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach. The primary comparison was stem cell injection compared with placebo injection. The primary time point for pain, function and quality of life was three to six months, and the end of the trial period for participant-reported success, joint structure changes and adverse event outcomes. Major outcomes were pain, function, quality of life, global assessment of success, radiographic joint progression, withdrawals due to adverse events and serious adverse events.
MAIN RESULTS: We found 25 randomised trials (1341 participants) comparing stem cell injections with placebo injection (eight trials), no treatment or usual care (analgesia, weight loss and exercise) (two trials), glucocorticoid injection (one trial), hyaluronic acid injection (seven trials), platelet-rich plasma injections (two trials), oral acetaminophen (paracetamol) (one trial), non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs plus physical therapy plus hyaluronic acid injection (one trial) and stem cell injection plus intra-articular co-intervention versus co-intervention alone (three trials) in people with osteoarthritis of the knee. Trials were predominantly small, with sample sizes ranging from 6 to 252 participants, with only two trials having more than 100 participants. The average age of participants across trials ranged from 51 to 66 years, and symptom duration varied from one to 10 years. Placebo-controlled trials were largely free from bias, while most trials without a placebo control were susceptible to performance and detection biases. Here, we limit reporting to the main comparison, stem cell injection versus placebo injection. Compared with placebo injection, stem cell injection may slightly improve pain and function up to six months after treatment. Mean pain (0 to 10 scale, 0 no pain) was 4.5 out of 10 points with placebo injection and 1.2 points better (2.5 points better to 0 points better) with stem cell injection (I2 = 80%; 7 studies, 445 participants). Mean function (0 to 100 scale, 0 best function) was 46.3 points with placebo injection and 14.2 points better (25.3 points better to 3.1 points better) with stem cell injection (I2 = 82%; 7 studies, 432 participants). We are uncertain whether stem cell injections improve quality of life or increase the number of people who report treatment success compared to placebo injection, because the certainty of the evidence was very low. Mean quality of life was 45.3 points with placebo injection and 22.8 points better (18.0 points worse to 63.7 points better) with stem cell injection (I2 = 96%; 2 studies, 288 participants) at up to six months follow-up. At the end of follow-up, 89/168 participants (530 per 1000) in the placebo injection group reported treatment success compared with 126/180 participants (683 per 1000) in the stem cell injection group (risk ratio (RR) 1.29, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.53; I2 = 0%; 4 trials, 348 participants). We downgraded the evidence to low certainty for pain and function due to indirectness (as the source, method of preparation and dose of stem cells varied across studies), and suspected publication bias (up to three larger RCTs have been conducted but withdrawn prior to reporting of results). For quality of life and treatment success, we further downgraded the evidence to very low certainty due to imprecision in addition to indirectness and suspected publication bias. We are uncertain of the potential harms associated with stem cell injection, as there were very low event rates for serious adverse events. At the end of follow-up, 5/219 participants (23 per 1000) in the placebo injection group experienced serious adverse events compared with 4/242 participants (16 per 1000) in the stem cell injection group (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.20 to 2.64; I2 = 0%; 7 trials, 461 participants) and there were no reported withdrawals due to adverse events. We downgraded the evidence to very low certainty due to indirectness, suspected publication bias and imprecision. Radiographic progression was not assessed in any of the included studies.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Compared with placebo injections and based upon low-certainty evidence, stem cell injections for people with knee osteoarthritis may slightly improve pain and function. We are uncertain of the effects of stem cell injections on quality of life or the number who report treatment success. Although the putative benefits of stem cell therapies for osteoarthritis include potential regenerative effects on damaged tissues, particularly articular cartilage, we remain uncertain of the effect of stem cell injections on structural progression in the knee (measured by radiographic appearance). There is also uncertainty regarding the safety of stem cell injections. Serious adverse events were infrequently reported, although all invasive joint procedures (including injections) carry a small risk of septic arthritis. The risk of other important harms, including potential concerns related to the use of a therapy with the theoretical capacity to promote cell growth, or to the use of allogeneic cells, remains unknown.

documents.title: Vitamin D supplementation for women during pregnancy.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy may help improve maternal and neonatal health outcomes (such as fewer preterm birth and low birthweight babies) and reduce the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes (such as severe postpartum haemorrhage).
OBJECTIVES: To examine whether vitamin D supplementation alone or in combination with calcium or other vitamins and minerals given to women during pregnancy can safely improve certain maternal and neonatal outcomes.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Trials Register (which includes results of comprehensive searches of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and relevant conference proceedings) (3 December 2022). We also searched the reference lists of retrieved studies.
SELECTION CRITERIA: Randomised and quasi-randomised trials evaluating the effect of supplementation with vitamin D alone or in combination with other micronutrients for women during pregnancy in comparison to placebo or no intervention.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: Two review authors independently i) assessed the eligibility of studies against the inclusion criteria, ii) assessed trustworthiness based on pre-defined criteria of scientific integrity, iii) extracted data from included studies, and iv) assessed the risk of bias of the included studies. We assessed the certainty of the evidence using the GRADE approach.
MAIN RESULTS: The previous version of this review included 30 studies; in this update, we have removed 20 of these studies to 'awaiting classification' following assessments of trustworthiness, one study has been excluded, and one new study included. This current review has a total of 10 included studies, 117 excluded studies, 34 studies in awaiting assessment, and seven ongoing studies. We used the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of the evidence. This removal of the studies resulted in evidence that was downgraded to low-certainty or very low-certainty due to study design limitations, inconsistency between studies, and imprecision. Supplementation with vitamin D compared to no intervention or a placebo A total of eight studies involving 2313 pregnant women were included in this comparison. We assessed four studies as having a low risk of bias for most domains and four studies as having high risk or unclear risk of bias for most domains. The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of supplementation with vitamin D during pregnancy compared to placebo or no intervention on pre-eclampsia (risk ratio (RR) 0.53, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.21 to 1.33; 1 study, 165 women), gestational diabetes (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.03 to 8.28; 1 study, 165 women), preterm birth (< 37 weeks) (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.25 to 2.33; 3 studies, 1368 women), nephritic syndrome (RR 0.17, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.06; 1 study, 135 women), or hypercalcaemia (1 study; no cases reported). Supplementation with vitamin D during pregnancy may reduce the risk of severe postpartum haemorrhage; however, only one study reported this outcome (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.91; 1 study, 1134 women; low-certainty evidence) and may reduce the risk of low birthweight; however, the upper CI suggests that an increase in risk cannot be ruled out (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.08; 3 studies, 371 infants; low-certainty evidence). Supplementation with vitamin D + calcium compared to no intervention or a placebo One study involving 84 pregnant women was included in this comparison. Overall, this study was at moderate to high risk of bias. Pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, and maternal adverse events were not reported. The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of supplementation with vitamin D and calcium on preterm birth (RR not estimable; very low-certainty evidence) or for low birthweight (RR 1.45, 95% CI 0.14 to 14.94; very low-certainty evidence) compared to women who received placebo or no intervention. Supplementation with vitamin D + calcium + other vitamins and minerals versus calcium + other vitamins and minerals (but no vitamin D) One study involving 1298 pregnant women was included in this comparison. We assessed this study as having a low risk of bias in all domains. Pre-eclampsia was not reported. The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of supplementation with vitamin D, calcium, and other vitamins and minerals during pregnancy compared to no vitamin D on gestational diabetes (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.10 to 1.73; very low-certainty evidence), maternal adverse events (hypercalcaemia no events and hypercalciuria RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.02 to 3.97; very low-certainty evidence), preterm birth (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.59; low-certainty evidence), or low birthweight (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.51; low-certainty evidence).
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: This updated review using the trustworthy assessment tool removed 21 studies from the previous update and added one new study for a total of 10 included studies. In this setting, supplementation with vitamin D alone compared to no intervention or a placebo resulted in very uncertain evidence on pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, or nephritic syndrome. It may reduce the risk of severe postpartum haemorrhage; however, only one study reported this outcome. It may also reduce the risk of low birthweight; however, the upper CI suggests that an increase in risk cannot be ruled out. Supplementation with vitamin D and calcium versus placebo or no intervention resulted in very uncertain evidence on preterm birth and low birthweight. Pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, and maternal adverse events were not reported in the only study included in this comparison. Supplementation with vitamin D + calcium + other vitamins and minerals versus calcium + other vitamins and minerals (but no vitamin D) resulted in very uncertain evidence on gestational diabetes and maternal adverse events (hypercalciuria) and uncertain evidence on preterm birth and low birthweight. Pre-eclampsia was not reported in the only study included in this comparison. All findings warrant further research. Additional rigorous, high-quality, and larger randomised trials are required to evaluate the effects of vitamin D supplementation in pregnancy, particularly in relation to the risk of maternal adverse events.

documents.title: Sodium-glucose co-transporter protein 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors for people with chronic kidney disease and diabetes.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diabetes is associated with high risks of premature chronic kidney disease (CKD), cardiovascular diseases, cardiovascular death and impaired quality of life. People with diabetes are more likely to develop kidney impairment, and approximately one in three adults with diabetes have CKD. People with CKD and diabetes experience a substantially higher risk of cardiovascular outcomes. Sodium-glucose co-transporter protein 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have shown potential effects in preventing kidney and cardiovascular outcomes in people with CKD and diabetes. However, new trials are emerging rapidly, and evidence synthesis is essential to summarising cumulative evidence.
OBJECTIVES: This review aimed to assess the benefits and harms of SGLT2 inhibitors for people with CKD and diabetes.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Register of Studies up to 17 November 2023 using a search strategy designed by an Information Specialist. Studies in the Register are continually identified through regular searches of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, conference proceedings, the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) Search Portal and ClinicalTrials.gov.
SELECTION CRITERIA: Randomised controlled studies were eligible if they evaluated SGLT2 inhibitors versus placebo, standard care or other glucose-lowering agents in people with CKD and diabetes. CKD includes all stages (from 1 to 5), including dialysis patients.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: Two authors independently extracted data and assessed the study risk of bias. Treatment estimates were summarised using random effects meta-analysis and expressed as a risk ratio (RR) or mean difference (MD), with a corresponding 95% confidence interval (CI). Confidence in the evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. The primary review outcomes were all-cause death, 3-point and 4-point major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), fatal or nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI), fatal or nonfatal stroke, and kidney failure.
MAIN RESULTS: Fifty-three studies randomising 65,241 people with CKD and diabetes were included. SGLT2 inhibitors with or without other background treatments were compared to placebo, standard care, sulfonylurea, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors, or insulin. In the majority of domains, the risks of bias in the included studies were low or unclear. No studies evaluated the treatment in children or in people treated with dialysis. No studies compared SGLT2 inhibitors with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists or tirzepatide. Compared to placebo, SGLT2 inhibitors decreased the risk of all-cause death (20 studies, 44,397 participants: RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78 to 0.94; I2 = 0%; high certainty) and cardiovascular death (16 studies, 43,792 participants: RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.93; I2 = 29%; high certainty). Compared to placebo, SGLT2 inhibitors probably make little or no difference to the risk of fatal or nonfatal MI (2 studies, 13,726 participants: RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.14; I2 = 24%; moderate certainty), and fatal or nonfatal stroke (2 studies, 13,726 participants: RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.30; I2 = 0%; moderate certainty). Compared to placebo, SGLT2 inhibitors probably decrease 3-point MACE (7 studies, 38,320 participants: RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.98; I2 = 46%; moderate certainty), and 4-point MACE (4 studies, 23,539 participants: RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.96; I2 = 77%; moderate certainty), and decrease hospital admission due to heart failure (6 studies, 28,339 participants: RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.79; I2 = 17%; high certainty). Compared to placebo, SGLT2 inhibitors may decrease creatinine clearance (1 study, 132 participants: MD -2.63 mL/min, 95% CI -5.19 to -0.07; low certainty) and probably decrease the doubling of serum creatinine (2 studies, 12,647 participants: RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.89; I2 = 53%; moderate certainty). SGLT2 inhibitors decrease the risk of kidney failure (6 studies, 11,232 participants: RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.79; I2 = 0%; high certainty), and kidney composite outcomes (generally reported as kidney failure, kidney death with or without ≥ 40% decrease in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)) (7 studies, 36,380 participants: RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.78; I2 = 25%; high certainty) compared to placebo. Compared to placebo, SGLT2 inhibitors incur less hypoglycaemia (16 studies, 28,322 participants: RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.89 to 0.98; I2 = 0%; high certainty), and hypoglycaemia requiring third-party assistance (14 studies, 26,478 participants: RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.88; I2 = 0%; high certainty), and probably decrease the withdrawal from treatment due to adverse events (15 studies, 16,622 participants: RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.08; I2 = 16%; moderate certainty). The effects of SGLT2 inhibitors on eGFR, amputation and fracture were uncertain. No studies evaluated the effects of treatment on fatigue, life participation, or lactic acidosis. The effects of SGLT2 inhibitors compared to standard care alone, sulfonylurea, DPP-4 inhibitors, or insulin were uncertain.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: SGLT2 inhibitors alone or added to standard care decrease all-cause death, cardiovascular death, and kidney failure and probably decrease major cardiovascular events while incurring less hypoglycaemia compared to placebo in people with CKD and diabetes.

documents.title: The role of estimated glucose disposal rate in predicting cardiovascular risk among general and diabetes mellitus population: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Estimated glucose disposal rate (eGDR) is a measure of insulin sensitivity. While recent evidence suggests its role in cardiovascular risk assessment in Type 1 diabetes, its associations with cardiovascular disease (CVD), diabetic microvascular complications (DMC), and mortality across different populations remain unclear.
METHODS: We systematically searched Medline, EMBASE, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library up to September 1st, 2024, following PRISMA guidelines. We examined associations between eGDR and CVD, DMC (including diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy, and peripheral neuropathy), and all-cause mortality using random-effects models. Secondary analysis assessed mean eGDR levels in diabetes populations.
RESULTS: Nineteen observational studies (185,810 participants) examined clinical outcomes, while 50 studies reported mean eGDR values. In patients with Type 1 diabetes (T1DM), each 1-unit (mg/kg/min) increase in eGDR was associated with lower risks of CVD (HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.69-0.87; I2 = 68%) and all-cause mortality (HR 0.83; 95% CI 0.79-0.88; I2 = 0%). The association between eGDR and DMC in T1DM was not statistically significant (HR 0.86; 95% CI 0.72-1.03; I2 = 25%). In patients with Type 2 diabetes (T2DM), each 1-unit (mg/kg/min) increase in eGDR was associated with reduced all-cause mortality (HR 0.90; 95% CI 0.84-0.97; I2 = 62%). Similarly, in the general population, each 1-unit (mg/kg/min) increase in eGDR was associated with decreased mortality risk (HR 0.88; 95% CI 0.82-0.94; I2 = 48%). The pooled mean eGDR was higher in patients with T1DM (8.19 mg/kg/min; 95% CI 7.81-8.57; I2 = 99%) compared to those with T2DM (7.03 mg/kg/min; 95% CI 4.89-9.17; I2 = 100%).
CONCLUSIONS: Higher eGDR levels were consistently associated with lower risks of CVD and mortality in T1DM, with similar associations observed for mortality in T2DM. In the general population, higher eGDR levels were associated with reduced mortality risk. The relationship between eGDR and DMC requires further investigation, particularly in T2DM. These findings suggest eGDR's potential utility as a risk assessment tool, though its clinical application may vary across different populations.
documents.conclusions: Higher eGDR levels were consistently associated with lower risks of CVD and mortality in T1DM, with similar associations observed for mortality in T2DM. In the general population, higher eGDR levels were associated with reduced mortality risk. The relationship between eGDR and DMC requires further investigation, particularly in T2DM. These findings suggest eGDR's potential utility as a risk assessment tool, though its clinical application may vary across different populations.

In 2021, 529 million people worldwide were living with diabetes, with projections suggesting an increase to over 1.3 billion by 2050 [ 2 ]. This trend highlights the escalating global burden of diabetes. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) and diabetic microvascular complications (DMC) remain the primary causes of morbidity and mortality in people with diabetes [ 3 , 4 ]. CVD, including atherosclerosis, coronary artery disease, and stroke, accounts for the majority of deaths, with people with diabetes showing significantly higher risk compared to the general population [ 5 ]. This elevated risk stems from the complex interplay between chronic hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, and metabolic dysregulation [ 6 ]. Similarly, DMC—comprising diabetic retinopathy (DR), diabetic nephropathy (DN), and diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN)—substantially impact quality of life [ 7 ]. Early identification and management of these complications are crucial for preventing irreversible damage and improving patient outcomes. Insulin resistance (IR) plays a fundamental role in vascular complications and adverse outcomes among people with diabetes [ 8 – 10 ]. While the euglycemic-hyperinsulinemic clamp technique remains the gold standard for assessing insulin sensitivity [ 11 – 13 ], its clinical application is limited by complexity, cost, and invasive nature. The estimated glucose disposal rate (eGDR) has emerged as a practical surrogate measure of insulin sensitivity, calculated using readily available clinical parameters: waist-to-hip ratio (WHR), waist circumference (WC), or body mass index (BMI), along with hypertension status (HTN) and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) [ 12 ]. The development and validation history of eGDR merit careful consideration when interpreting its applications across different populations. Initially validated against the hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp in Type 1 diabetes (T1DM) [ 12 ], eGDR demonstrated a strong correlation with insulin sensitivity in this population. Subsequent clamp studies validated its utility in Type 2 diabetes (T2DM) [ 14 ]. Although direct clamp validation in the general population is currently lacking, the biological plausibility of eGDR as a marker of insulin resistance is supported by its individual components, as hypertension, anthropometric measures, and HbA1c are closely associated with insulin resistance and cardiovascular risk in non-diabetic individuals [ 15 – 20 ]. Recent evidence has demonstrated eGDR's utility as a risk stratification tool [ 21 ], particularly for cardiovascular outcomes in T1DM, as shown in a recent systematic review [ 22 ]. Building upon existing evidence, some important questions remain to be addressed. While recent reviews have examined eGDR's relationship with cardiovascular outcomes in T1DM, less is known about its associations with both cardiovascular and DMC across different populations, and typical eGDR values in various population groups have not been systematically summarized. Therefore, our systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to examine associations between eGDR and cardiovascular disease, DMC, and mortality in people with T1DM, T2DM, and the general population. These findings may contribute to our understanding of eGDR's utility in clinical risk assessment across different populations. Methods This systematic review and meta-analysis adhered to the guidelines established in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) 2020 [ 23 ] (Additional file 1: Table 1). We registered the protocol with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews Database (PROSPERO) under the registration number CRD42024527263. The PRISMA flow diagram is shown in Fig. 1 . Fig. 1 The PRISMA flow diagram Literature search and selection Two independent reviewers searched the Medline, EMBASE, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library databases with no linguistic constraints from inception up to Sep 1st, 2024. Both MeSH terms and free-text terms were utilized in a combination of four key term blocks:"eGDR,""CVD,""diabetic microangiopathy,"and"mortality"(Additional file 1: Table 2). Adhering to research integrity standards, we included all observational studies that furnished insights into associations between eGDR and the risk of CVD,DMC, and mortality. Studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) they were observational studies, including cross-sectional, retrospective and prospective cohort studies, or randomized controlled trials (RCTs); (2) they enrolled the general population or patients with DM; (3) studies presented data on the association between eGDR and the risk of CVD, DMC, and mortality. Studies were excluded if they: (1) involved nonhuman subjects; (2) were case reports (unless N > 10), editorials, protocols, commentaries, abstracts, or registered trials without results; or (3) lacked a clear methodology for data extraction. We employed a hierarchical approach in our analysis strategy. For cohort studies reporting hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), we conducted quantitative meta-analyses using either directly reported per-unit HRs or standardized HRs derived from categorical data using established dose–response methods. Cohort studies meeting inclusion criteria but lacking sufficient data for HR standardization were included in the narrative synthesis. Regarding cross-sectional studies, we excluded them from meta-analyses when comparable cohort data were available for the same population and outcome. However, in cases where cohort data were insufficient or unavailable, we incorporated cross-sectional studies into the narrative synthesis to provide complementary evidence on eGDR-outcome associations. Definitions of eGDR and outcomes The eGDR (mg/kg/min) was determined using the following formulas: A eGDR WHR = 24.31 – (12.22 * WHR) – (3.29 * HT) – (0.57 * HbA1c). B eGDR WC = 21.16 – (0.09 × WC) – (3.41 × HTN) – (0.55 × HbA1c). C eGDR BMI = 19.02 – (0.22 × BMI) – (3.26 × HTN) – (0.61 × HbA1c). The waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) is calculated by dividing the waist circumference by the hip circumference. Hypertension is a binary variable indicating the presence (1) or absence (0) of hypertension. HbA1c is expressed as a percentage. Hypertension is defined as either treatment with antihypertensive medication or systolic blood pressure (SBP) greater than 140 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure (DBP) greater than 90 mm Hg [ 12 , 14 ]. This meta-analysis focused on two primary objectives: first, to explore the association between eGDR and the risk of CVD, DMC and mortality; and second, to estimate the overall mean level of eGDR in different populations. CVD was primarily defined using standardized diagnostic codes from the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10), encompassing coronary artery disease (CAD, I20–I25), stroke (I60–I69), and peripheral arterial disease (PAD, I70–I79). While one study included self-reported CVD outcomes [ 24 ], we systematically addressed this definitional heterogeneity through stratified analyses. DMC includes DR, diabetic nephropathy (DN), and diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN). Mortality was defined as all-cause mortality. Detailed definitions of clinical outcomes in each study are presented in Additional file 1: Table 3. Data extraction and quality assessment Two reviewers independently scrutinized the titles, abstracts, and full texts of studies to determine eligibility. Data extracted include study characteristics such as authors, study design, location, sample size, data source, timing of data collection, participant demographics (age and sex), duration of DM, duration of follow-up, and eGDR levels. Event counts, crude and adjusted HRs, along with their 95% CIs for each outcome, were also recorded. For studies using overlapping cohorts but reporting on distinct outcomes, all relevant studies were incorporated into the pooled analysis for their respective outcomes. Any discrepancies and disagreements in the data extraction process were resolved through collaborative discussion, with a third researcher examining the original data to reach a consensus. A validated 14-item quality assessment tool developed by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) was used to assess the quality of each study (available at https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health-topics/study-quality-assessment-tools ). Each item was categorized as "yes" (1 point), "no" (0 points), "not reported", or "not applicable." A score of 1 point was assigned if the item was adequately described, and 0 points if it lacked sufficient description or did not meet the quality criteria. "Not reported" was used when the item lacked a clear description, and "not applicable" when the assessment criteria could not be met. The maximum attainable score was 14 points for longitudinal studies and 11 points for observational and cross-sectional studies. For longitudinal studies, scores were categorized as high quality (> 9 points), medium quality (4–9 points), and low quality (< 4 points). For cross-sectional studies, high quality was defined as > 7 points, medium quality as 3–7 points, and low quality as < 3 points. Medium- and low-quality studies were considered high-risk publications. Two independent reviewers conducted the evaluations, resolving any discrepancies through discussion. Data synthesis and statistical analyses We conducted quantitative synthesis using R software (version 3.4.0). HRs for CVD, DMC, and all-cause mortality were pooled using random-effects models. For cohort studies reporting HRs by eGDR quantiles, we standardized the effects to represent per-unit increases in eGDR using established dose–response methodology. This transformation required the following data elements from each study: eGDR category boundaries, event counts, participant numbers per category, adjusted HRs, and their 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The methodology assumed normally distributed exposure variables and log-linear exposure-outcome relationships [ 25 , 26 ]. We employed the DerSimonian-Laird random-effects method to synthesize the reported HRs and their 95% CIs [ 27 ]. For studies reporting multiple effect estimates for the same outcome, we selected the most relevant adjusted estimate to avoid unit-of-analysis errors (Additional file 1: Table 4). A separate meta-analysis was conducted to pool the mean eGDR levels across studies using untransformed means (MRAW) and standard deviations (SDs). The overall eGDR estimates and their 95% CIs were calculated using inverse variance weighting [ 28 ]. Results were visualized through forest plots, and between-study heterogeneity was quantified using I 2 statistics and tau 2 with corresponding 95% CIs [ 27 , 29 ]. We conducted comprehensive subgroup analyses to investigate potential sources of heterogeneity across predefined stratification factors, including mean age (≤ 30 versus > 30 years), geographical location (Europe versus North America), study site characteristics (single-center versus multicenter), sample size (≤ 1000 versus > 1000 participants), follow-up duration (≤ 10 versus > 10 years), diabetes duration (≤ 20 versus > 20 years), and eGDR formulas (eGDR WHR , eGDR WC , or eGDR BMI ). To evaluate the robustness of our findings, we performed three distinct sensitivity analyses. The first analysis examined the stability of risk estimates for CVD, DMC, and mortality across three levels of covariate adjustment: Model I (unadjusted or adjusted for age and sex only), Model II (Model I plus diabetes duration), and Model III (Model II plus demographic factors and conventional CVD risk factors at baseline). We also performed leave-one-out sensitivity analyses by sequentially excluding individual studies to examine their influence on the pooled estimates and identify potential outliers. Third, considering the variation in CVD definitions across studies, we assessed the impact of this heterogeneity by specifically addressing studies that relied on self-reported CVD. For studies included in the meta-analysis, we performed additional sensitivity analyses to evaluate their impact on the overall pooled estimates. For studies included in the narrative synthesis, we provided detailed explanations in the corresponding sections to account for the potential limitations associated with self-reported CVD. Reporting bias assessment and certainty assessment A funnel plot and Egger's test were planned to assess publication bias and small-study effects if more than six studies reported data on the same outcome [ 30 ]. The Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach [ 31 ] was used to evaluate the certainty of the evidence, categorizing it as high, moderate, low, or very low based on evaluation criteria. Results Study selection Our literature search initially identified 1,242 records. After removing duplicates and screening titles and abstracts, 94 articles were selected for full-text review. Following detailed evaluation, 25 articles were excluded: 8 due to duplicate data sources and 17 due to irrelevant outcomes (Additional file 1: Table 5). The final analysis included 69 studies for systematic review, of which 63 were eligible for quantitative synthesis and 6 were eligible for narrative synthesis (Fig. 1 ). Among the included studies, 19 investigated the associations between eGDR and clinical outcomes (CVD, DMC, and all-cause mortality), while 50 studies reported mean eGDR values in diabetic populations. Study characteristics Again, the included 19 observational studies examined the associations between eGDR and clinical outcomes (CVD, DMC, and mortality) (Table 1 ). These comprised 17 cohort studies and 2 cross-sectional studies, with a total enrollment of 185,810 participants. The geographical distribution of the studies was diverse: six from North America (five studies conducted in the United States and one study conducted across the United States and Canada), seven from Europe (four Swedish, one Italian, one Finnish, and one study from the Netherlands), five from Asia (all conducted in China), and one study conducted across the United States and Italy. Individual study sample sizes varied considerably, ranging from 366 to 104,697 participants. For the analysis of mean eGDR levels, we included 50 studies (Additional file 1: Table 6), with 46 studies focusing on T1DM and four on T2DM. Among the 50 studies included in the analysis of mean eGDR levels, 28 (56%) achieved "high quality" ratings, while the remaining 22 (44%) were assessed as "medium quality"(Additional file 1: Table 8). eGDR and the risk of CVD Nine studies investigated the association between eGDR and CVD risk across different populations. Of these, six studies conducted in patients with T1DM (Helmink 2021 [ 35 ], Garofolo 2020 [ 8 ], Miller 2019 [ 36 ], Nystrom 2018 [ 37 ], Kilpatrick 2007 [ 38 ], Olson 2002 [ 39 ]) were included in a meta-analysis. Two studies in patients with T2DM (Zabala 2021 [ 41 ], Nystrom 2017 [ 47 ]) were included in a narrative analysis, while one study conducted in the general population (Zhang 2024 [ 48 ]) was also included in a narrative analysis (Table 1 ). Our findings revealed that each unit increase in eGDR was associated with an HR of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.69–0.87, I 2 = 68%, τ 2 = 0.0127, p < 0.01), indicating a significant protective effect against CVD risk (Fig. 2 A). Subgroup analyses in T1DM patients demonstrated the consistency of this protective association across various stratification factors, including age, geographical location, study center, sample size, follow-up duration, and eGDR formula. Notably, studies using the eGDR formula A exhibited higher heterogeneity (I 2 = 80%, p < 0.01) compared to those using formula C (I 2 = 0%, p = 0.59), suggesting that the choice of eGDR formula may be a potential source of heterogeneity (Table 2 ).
